column4: God seizes Pharaoh with punishment of the later and the former; the consequence immediately overturns his claim to be the highest lord and restores the two-life scale.
Pharaoh's reversal is made an admonitory sign for whoever fears, linking the cited scene to the fear that receives reminder in Surah 87.
The question whether humans are harder to create than the heaven God built redirects attention from Pharaoh's assumed height to the Creator of actual height.
The coming overwhelming event is called the greatest catastrophe, placing the greatness root immediately before remembrance, exposed Hell, and the low-life choice.
On that day the human being remembers what he strove for; remembrance now discloses the life-choice whose judgment follows.
Hell is made plainly visible to every observer just before the one who transgressed and preferred worldly life is identified.
The revelation is taught by one mighty in power, identifying the agent whose strength, stance, and appearance at the high horizon are described in 53:6-7.
The discourse is the word conveyed by a noble messenger, identifying the same revelation-bearer whose horizon appearance is stated in 81:23.
The messenger has power and an established station with the Lord of the Throne, giving rightful rank and strength to the figure seen on the horizon.
The Prophet saw the messenger on the clear horizon, a direct parallel to the high-horizon figure in 53:7 and to the dictionary's emerging silhouette.
No person's favor is being repaid by the giver; this excludes a lower reciprocal motive before 92:20 names the Most High Lord as his sole aim.
The giver who seeks the face of his Most High Lord will be satisfied, completing the movement beyond wealth and human recompense.
God rewards the worshippers of 24:37 according to their best deeds and increases them from His bounty, supplying the higher return for leaving trade subordinate to remembrance.
The human being transgresses, introducing the counterfeit upward motion inside the surah that began by naming the creating Lord.
Seeing himself self-sufficient explains the transgression in 96:6; imagined independence is the inward form of claiming height for oneself.
The return is to your Lord, setting the final horizon above the self-sufficiency that produced transgression in 96:6-7.
People take religious leaders and the Messiah as lords besides God; glorifying Him above their association clears the title “Lord” of creaturely seizure.
The claim that God takes a son is answered by declaring Him transcendent; this gives the section's definition of tasbih a specific false description to remove.
After asking whether alleged partners create, provide, kill, or revive, the ayah glorifies and exalts God above them, joining transcendence to uniquely divine acts.
God is glorified above what people describe, a direct formulation of tasbih as clearing Him of every unworthy attribution.
The question whether they possess a god other than God ends by glorifying Him above their partners, reserving lordship and height for Him.
The angels glorify God and disown the people who worshipped them, showing exalted servants refusing the divine rank humans projected onto them.

When people demand that the Prophet ascend into heaven and bring down a book, he answers by glorifying his Lord and affirming that he is only a human messenger; claimed human ascent is bounded by divine transcendence.
Protected houses of worship are places where God's name is mentioned much; their preservation concretely sustains the raised-name space described in 24:36.
Preventing God's name from being remembered in places of worship and seeking their ruin is the precise reversal of raising houses for His name and tasbih.
The Prophet is told to remain with those calling their Lord and seeking His face, and not to let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment; remembrance and the low-life choice meet directly.
Hearts recoil when God alone is mentioned but rejoice when lesser objects are mentioned, exposing a reversed hierarchy of remembrance.
“Remember Me and I will remember you” makes remembrance reciprocal divine acknowledgment rather than a mere utterance, supporting dhikr's honor-bearing sense.
After being told to remember God intensely, some people ask only for this world and have no share in the hereafter; low-life desire stands inside a remembrance scene.
The balanced prayer asks for good in both this world and the hereafter and protection from Fire, correcting the one-horizon request in 2:200.
Desired possessions are presented as the adornment of worldly life, while the beautiful return is with God; attraction and destination are placed on different levels.
The Prophet is told to announce what is better than worldly adornment: lasting gardens, purified spouses, and God's approval.
Those who desire the reward of this world and those who desire the reward of the hereafter are explicitly distinguished, making preference a chosen horizon of recompense.
Those who sell worldly life for the hereafter are summoned to struggle, reversing the exchange made by people who buy the low life.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that the rewards of both this world and the hereafter are with God, setting a boundary against treating nearness as the only available good.
Worldly life is likened to rain-fed growth that reaches full adornment and is suddenly reduced as though it had not flourished yesterday, a close nonlexical parallel to passing pasture.
Those who respond well receive good in this world, but the home of the hereafter is better; the ayah preserves worldly good while ranking the final home above it.
A person promised a good fulfillment is set against one merely given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment, separating lasting promise from present possession.
The command to seek the final home with what God has given while not forgetting one's worldly share marks the boundary between ranking the hereafter higher and denying lawful present life.
Whoever seeks the harvest of the hereafter receives increase, while the seeker of worldly harvest receives only some of it and no final share.
Worldly life is play and diversion, whereas faith and reverence receive their reward; present possession is denied the power to measure true rank.
After worldly growth and debris in 57:20, believers are told to race toward forgiveness and a garden as wide as heaven and earth, supplying the enduring destination beyond the fading scene.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from God's remembrance; immediate attachments and dhikr are presented as competing orientations.
Wealth and children are only a trial, while a great reward is with God; possessed greatness is subordinated to bestowed greatness.
People know only the outward surface of worldly life while remaining heedless of the hereafter, making nearness also an epistemic limitation.
The Prophet must turn from one who turns from God's reminder and desires only worldly life; dhikr and low-life preference are direct alternatives.
That worldly horizon is called the limit of their knowledge, while the Lord knows who strays and who is guided; nearness confines understanding as well as desire.
The heirs of scripture take the goods of “this lower/nearer” existence while presuming forgiveness, an explicit adjectival use of أدنى for morally cheap present gain.
Moses asks whether the people would exchange what is lower for what is better, directly stating the value contrast carried by the section's discussion of أدنى.
People made God's signs an object of ridicule and were deceived by worldly life; the low horizon becomes the agent of their false estimate.
A good word is a good tree with firm root and branch in the sky, giving elevated speech a visible upward form and stable ground.
A bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, the downward and rootless counterpart to the ascending good word in 14:24.
The Quran is in the Mother of the Book with God, exalted and wise; revealed remembrance itself receives a true high station.
The account of how God speaks to humans ends by naming Him High and Wise, grounding descending revelation in the exaltation of its speaker.
God apportions worldly livelihood and raises some above others in degrees for mutual service, yet His mercy is better than what they accumulate; worldly rank is relativized within the ayah.
After Abraham rejects setting lights as lords, God says He raises in degrees whom He wills; true elevation is bestowed after false celestial lordship is refused.
God makes people successors on earth and raises some above others in degrees to test them, defining worldly elevation as probation rather than possession.
God favors some messengers over others and raises some in degrees, presenting rank as His grant even among honored servants.
God tells Jesus that He will raise him to Himself and purify him from the disbelievers, joining elevation to divine action and purification.
Rather than Jesus being mastered by his enemies, God raised him to Himself; creaturely plots are bounded by divine elevation.
The recipient of the right-hand record enters a high garden, making eschatological height the outcome of accepted life rather than claimed status.
The high garden's fruit clusters are near, joining height and nearness as harmonized gifts and contrasting this nearness with the morally low worldly life.
Faces are humbled on the coming day, an eschatological lowering that strips away assumed worldly elevation.
Those humbled faces enter a scorching fire, supplying the fire-side of the passage's later contrast with a high garden.
Other faces are in a high garden, giving true height as an awarded final dwelling opposite the humbled faces and fire.
Raised couches furnish the high garden, making its elevation a concrete created gift rather than a human claim.
Garden shade draws near and its fruit clusters are lowered within reach; true nearness is received through a merciful lowering in the final abode.
Hypocrites occupy the lowest depth of the Fire, the direct downward opposite of the highest degrees promised to faithful workers.
After gardens and dwellings are promised, God's approval is called greater; divine pleasure outranks even the created reward.
Iblis is ordered down because the place is not for self-magnification and is expelled among the abased; assumed height produces literal and moral descent.
The arrogant are told to enter Hell's gates permanently, directly joining seized greatness to the fire-end of the section.
The faces of those who lied about God are darkened, and Hell is named the lodging of the arrogant; false description and self-greatness meet their reversal.
The arrogant are commanded into Hell's gates for permanent residence, making their chosen height end in the worst lodging.
Entering Hell's gates is again called the dwelling of the arrogant, a repeated Quranic judgment on creaturely greatness.
Pharaoh and his troops exalt themselves in the land without right and deny their return, identifying the attitude behind the tower ordered in 28:38.
God seizes Pharaoh and his troops and casts them into the sea, an abrupt downward reversal of the attempted ascent in 28:38-39.
Pharaoh makes his people light or foolish and they obey him; the social mechanism of his claimed superiority is the lowering of those beneath him.
At the fire Moses is told that the speaker is God, the Mighty, the Wise; the name identifies the Lord whose transcendence was declared in 27:8.
At judgment the earth shines with the light of its Lord, giving divine splendor a cosmic scene rather than locating majesty in a creature's flame.
The seven heavens, earth, and everything in them glorify God; tasbih becomes the universal response of the entire high-low creation.
All beings in heaven and earth, including birds spread in flight, know their prayer and glorification; the raised houses of 24:36 belong within a wider cosmic worship scene.
Thunder glorifies God with praise and the angels do so in awe, placing tasbih in a visibly and audibly high atmospheric scene.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord with praise and to be among those who prostrate, joining exaltation of God to bodily lowering.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord before sunrise and sunset and through the night, placing tasbih repeatedly along the horizon and daily arc.
Glorification with the Lord's praise is commanded before sunrise and sunset, joining the speaker stance to the horizon imagery developed in the section.
While standing under the Lord's watch, the Prophet is commanded to glorify Him with praise; worship, stance, and divine oversight meet.
Night glorification and the retreat of the stars extend the command of 52:48 into the celestial scene.
At the moment of victory the Prophet must glorify his Lord with praise and seek forgiveness, preventing success from becoming self-elevation.
True believers fall prostrate when reminded of the signs, glorify their Lord, and do not act arrogantly; low posture and tasbih directly reverse false height.
Angels surround the Throne glorifying their Lord with praise as judgment is completed, locating tasbih around the highest emblem of rule.
